title: Mock: Phone Screen
focus: Four timed rounds under real constraints. No notes, no editor autocomplete, talk out loud the whole time.

cards.title: Round 0: Warm-up
cards.trigger: Twenty minutes, two problems. If either takes more than ten minutes, that pattern is not yet automatic.
cards.recall: No notes. Before writing anything, say the pattern name and the complexity out loud, as if someone is listening. Then code. Then state the edge cases you handled.
template: # The four sentences you say before writing a line. Every round. Out loud.
#   1. 'Let me restate the problem to make sure I have it.'
#   2. 'The constraints are ..., so I am targeting ... complexity.'
#   3. 'This looks like a <pattern> problem because <trigger>.'
#   4. 'Before I code, the edge cases are: empty, single element, all duplicates.'
# If you cannot say sentence 3, you are not ready to code. Keep thinking.
keyInsights: Restating the problem catches a misreading before it costs you thirty minutes. It is not a formality
Naming the target complexity from the constraints signals seniority more than any single solution does
Warm-up rounds exist to get your hands moving. Do not skip them because the problems look easy
cards.trap: Silence. A correct solution written silently scores worse than a slightly worse solution narrated well. The interviewer is scoring communication explicitly.

cards.title: Round 1: Standard Medium
cards.trigger: Twenty-five minutes, one medium. This is the actual shape of a Google phone screen.
cards.recall: Pick ONE without looking at the others. Set a timer. Do not start coding until you have said the approach and the complexity out loud.
template: # Time budget for a 25-minute medium:
#   0:00 - 0:03   restate, clarify, ask about constraints and edge cases
#   0:03 - 0:07   approach out loud, complexity, get a nod before coding
#   0:07 - 0:18   write it, narrating the non-obvious lines only
#   0:18 - 0:23   trace one small example by hand, out loud
#   0:23 - 0:25   state the complexity again, and one thing you would improve
# If you are still silent at 0:07, you are behind. Say something, even
# if it is 'the brute force is O(n^2) and I am looking for better'.
keyInsights: Getting a nod on the approach before coding is what stops you from writing twenty lines in the wrong direction
Tracing an example by hand catches off-by-ones that reading the code will not
Naming an improvement at the end, even a small one, closes the interview on a strong note
cards.trap: Jumping straight to the optimal solution with no brute force stated. If the optimal is wrong you have nothing to fall back on, and you have shown no reasoning.

cards.title: Round 2: Medium with a Follow-Up
cards.trigger: Thirty-five minutes. Solve it, then answer the follow-up. The follow-up is the actual test.
cards.recall: Solve the problem, then immediately answer its follow-up as if asked. Do not look up the follow-up. If you cannot generate one yourself, you do not understand the problem well enough.
template: # Generate your own follow-up. The five that come up most:
#   1. 'Now the input is a stream and does not fit in memory.'
#   2. 'Now return the actual thing, not just its size or count.'
#   3. 'Now do it in O(1) space.'
#   4. 'Now the constraint is relaxed: negatives, duplicates, unbounded values.'
#   5. 'Now there are a million queries instead of one.'
# For each of your month's 150 problems, at least one of these applies.
keyInsights: The follow-up is where L4 is separated from L3. A clean base solution with a fumbled follow-up reads as memorisation
Reconstructing the answer, rather than its size, usually forces a different data structure. Notice that before they ask
'A million queries' almost always means precompute, and 'a stream' almost always means you cannot sort
cards.trap: Answering a follow-up by saying 'I would just modify the code'. Say specifically what changes and what it costs, or say you do not know. Vagueness scores worse than either.

cards.title: Round 3: Hard
cards.trigger: Forty minutes, one hard. The goal is not necessarily to finish. The goal is to make visible progress out loud.
cards.recall: Pick one you did NOT solve smoothly this month. Forty minutes on a clock. If you stall, narrate the stall: say what you have, what you need, and what you would try next.
template: # When you stall, say this rather than going quiet:
#   'Here is what I have: <the invariant or partial approach>.'
#   'Here is what I am missing: <the specific gap>.'
#   'Two things I would try: <A> and <B>. I will try <A> because <reason>.'
# A narrated stall is a hiring signal. A silent stall is a no-hire.
# And the fallback that is always available:
#   'Let me write the brute force first so we have something correct,
#    then optimise from there.'
keyInsights: Partial credit is real. An interviewer writes down what you demonstrated, not just whether it compiled
The brute-force fallback guarantees you leave with working code. Start it at the twenty-five minute mark if you are stuck
Hards are usually one insight away from a medium you know. Ask yourself which medium this resembles
cards.trap: Spending forty minutes searching for the elegant solution and submitting nothing. Correct and slow beats elegant and absent, every time.

cards.title: Debrief: Score Yourself
cards.trigger: Ten minutes. Grade the session honestly, and write down exactly one thing to fix.
cards.recall: Answer all six questions below in writing. Not in your head, in writing. Then pick the single weakest one and make it tomorrow's first task.
template: # Score each round 0 to 3. Be harsh.
#   1. Did I restate and clarify before coding?
#   2. Did I state the complexity BEFORE writing, not after?
#   3. Did I name the pattern, or did I stumble into it?
#   4. Did I go silent at any point for more than thirty seconds?
#   5. Did I trace an example by hand before declaring it done?
#   6. Could I answer the follow-up without looking anything up?
# Total out of 18. Below 12 means the gap is process, not knowledge.
# Then: the ONE fix for tomorrow. One. Not a list.
keyInsights: Most rejections at L4 are process failures, not knowledge failures. Silence, no complexity analysis, no edge cases
Writing the score down is what makes the pattern visible across months. Keeping it in your head does not
One fix per session. A list of six fixes is a list of zero fixes
cards.trap: Scoring yourself generously because you solved the problems. The problems are the easy part. Google is grading how you got there.
